variants.title: Launch-day spike
variants.context: A product launches with 4,000 req/s and one app server reaches 96% CPU in 90 seconds.
variants.constraint: Requests queue and the same server handles all work.
variants.question: What is the first fix you choose?
variants.expectedPattern: Run several identical stateless app servers and spread traffic across them.

variants.title: Nightly import burst
variants.context: A nightly job sends 12,000 API requests in 30 seconds and one server sits saturated.
variants.constraint: The services are stateful on a single node.
variants.question: What architectural pattern reduces the failure risk most cleanly?
variants.expectedPattern: Scale horizontally with stateless workers behind a shared entry point.

variants.title: Microservice rollout
variants.context: A new microservice is deployed and traffic to it jumps from 500 to 15,000 req/s.
variants.constraint: Only one service instance exists and it hits CPU limits.
variants.question: What should happen next?
variants.expectedPattern: Add more identical instances and route work across them.
wrongChoices: Move traffic to a single backup node
Keep all traffic on one host

variants.title: Background worker backlog
variants.context: A background worker is doing image processing and the queue is growing faster than it drains.
variants.constraint: One worker is overloaded while others are idle.
variants.question: Which operating model restores capacity?
variants.expectedPattern: Run multiple workers that all pull from the same work queue.
wrongChoices: Add more retries on the same task

variants.title: API traffic from one region
variants.context: An API in one region grows from 1k to 20k req/s, but all users hit the same app instance.
variants.constraint: The rest of the fleet does almost no work.
variants.question: What is the fundamental mismatch?
variants.expectedPattern: Traffic is not evenly distributed, so the fleet is underutilized.

variants.title: One crash takes the whole service down
variants.context: The app service keeps user session state in memory and loses all sessions when the process dies.
variants.constraint: The system is not stateless and cannot be rebuilt quickly.
variants.question: What is the design issue behind the outage?
variants.expectedPattern: Sessions and app state must be externalized or removed from process-local memory.

variants.title: Hot service with no redundancy
variants.context: One search service handles every request while other instances are maintained but unused.
variants.constraint: The entry path still targets a single endpoint.
variants.question: How do you improve resilience?
variants.expectedPattern: Distribute requests to a fleet and remove single-host routing.
wrongChoices: Add a bigger CPU on the same node

variants.title: Tricky burst from social traffic
variants.context: A product’s traffic spikes after a social media mention, but the app server pool is small and homogeneous.
variants.constraint: No instance is stateful and one instance can no longer keep up.
variants.question: What changes the system from fragile to resilient?
variants.expectedPattern: Add more stateless instances behind a shared entry route.

variants.title: Long-running job fan-out
variants.context: A service watches for new files and processes them one at a time, so latency grows with each upload.
variants.constraint: Work is serial and CPU-bound on a single instance.
variants.question: What is the cleanest fix?
variants.expectedPattern: Parallelize work across multiple stateless workers.
wrongChoices: Move to a single giant machine

variants.title: Election-day traffic surge
variants.context: Users hit a public API as a live event starts, and one app instance exceeds 100% CPU.
variants.constraint: The event is short but intense; capacity must be elastic.
variants.question: How do you prepare for this kind of event?
variants.expectedPattern: Add multiple stateless app instances in advance and route traffic to them.

variants.title: Server 1 is overloaded
variants.context: Three app servers are live, but 90% of traffic still routes to Server 1.
variants.constraint: The other servers are almost idle.
variants.question: What is the root cause?
variants.expectedPattern: Clients are bypassing a distribution layer and hitting one server directly.

variants.title: One server dies
variants.context: An instance fails in the middle of a traffic burst and requests start failing immediately.
variants.constraint: The remaining servers are healthy but not all traffic is rerouted.
variants.question: How do you route around the failure?
variants.expectedPattern: Add a load balancer with health checks that remove unhealthy nodes from rotation.
wrongChoices: Keep sending requests to the dead node

variants.title: Mobile clients bypass the public endpoint
variants.context: The app has two servers, but mobile traffic is still pointed at the old host directly.
variants.constraint: The app layer is horizontally scaled but not reachable through the load balancer.
variants.question: What completes the fix?
variants.expectedPattern: Send all traffic through the load balancer so distribution is centralized.

variants.title: Uneven traffic after a deployment
variants.context: A new version is deployed to two servers, but one receives 68% of the traffic.
variants.constraint: The balancing policy is not consistent and one node gets more than its share.
variants.question: What is the immediate design problem?
variants.expectedPattern: The routing policy is not distributing work evenly.

variants.title: Latency climbs after an app restart
variants.context: One app server is restarted and the traffic is still mostly directed to the old instance.
variants.constraint: Healthy nodes are available but get little traffic.
variants.question: What keeps the system unhealthy?
variants.expectedPattern: Long-lived client-targeting or stale routing still bypasses the balancing layer.

variants.title: All traffic hits one edge instance
variants.context: A single edge service is the main public door, but the remaining edges are not in rotation.
variants.constraint: The app is scaled yet not balanced.
variants.question: What is the best fix?
variants.expectedPattern: Use a reverse proxy or load balancer with health checks and failover.
wrongChoices: Use only round robin without health checks

variants.title: A region fails but no traffic shift happens
variants.context: A regional app server crashes, yet clients continue hitting the bad endpoint for a long time.
variants.constraint: There is a health check gap.
variants.question: Which property should the distribution layer provide?
variants.expectedPattern: Automatic removal of unhealthy targets from the rotation and rerouting.

variants.title: Traffic spins between two servers
variants.context: A two-node system alternates latency spikes even though the nodes are healthy.
variants.constraint: The routing algorithm is not aware of node health and session stickiness is weak.
variants.question: What should be improved?
variants.expectedPattern: Session-aware or health-aware balancing plus better backend utilization.

variants.title: Cascading failures after one crash
variants.context: During a moderate surge, one node dies and the rest absorb too much traffic until they also fail.
variants.constraint: The load balancer had no failover policy for partial failure.
variants.question: What design decision prevents this pattern?
variants.expectedPattern: Keep capacity above normal load and remove failed nodes aggressively.

variants.title: Traffic is uneven by geography
variants.context: Users in Europe are routed to one node while Asia goes to another, and one node is overloaded.
variants.constraint: The balancing layer is not aware of region or health.
variants.question: What is the correct balancing principle?
variants.expectedPattern: Balance by health and capacity, not simply by static rules or manual assignment.

variants.title: Read-heavy feed
variants.context: An app is serving a personalized feed with 95% reads and a single primary database becomes saturated.
variants.constraint: Almost all traffic is read-only and writes are relatively small.
variants.question: What is the most direct fix?
variants.expectedPattern: Add read replicas and send read traffic to them.
wrongChoices: Use a cache before the database

variants.title: Analytics report slows checkout
variants.context: A reporting service runs heavy queries on the same database and checkout transactions lock up.
variants.constraint: Reports are read-heavy and can tolerate lag.
variants.question: What should be moved?
variants.expectedPattern: Move the analytics queries to a read replica.
wrongChoices: Move reporting to the app tier

variants.title: User updates profile and instantly reads old data
variants.context: A user changes their profile and immediately refreshes. They see the prior version.
variants.constraint: Replication from primary to replica is asynchronous.
variants.question: What pattern solves it?
variants.expectedPattern: Read-your-own-writes routing or a fresh read path for that user.
wrongChoices: Move the user to a new server

variants.title: Hot read-only workload
variants.context: Most traffic is reading product pages, but one primary database is CPU-bound.
variants.constraint: Writes are modest and distributed among a few users.
variants.question: How do you relieve the bottleneck?
variants.expectedPattern: Use read replicas for the high-volume read path.
wrongChoices: Add more writes to the primary
Turn the app into a cache

variants.title: Followers are stale
variants.context: The app reads from replicas but a user expects a fresh view immediately after posting.
variants.constraint: Replication delay is measured in seconds, not milliseconds.
variants.question: What should you design around?
variants.expectedPattern: Bounded freshness for the user’s own writes, not global strong consistency.
wrongChoices: Force all reads to wait for full replication

variants.title: Single-source-of-truth cluster
variants.context: The product has multiple app servers that all do reads and writes on one database.
variants.constraint: The database is the bottleneck even though app traffic is okay.
variants.question: What is the best next step?
variants.expectedPattern: Separate reads from writes using replicas and a primary database.

variants.title: Page loads are slow despite healthy app servers
variants.context: The app tier is at 35% CPU, but end-user latency is 7 seconds.
variants.constraint: The system is waiting on database reads and writes.
variants.question: What is the bottleneck?
variants.expectedPattern: The primary database is overloaded with both reads and writes.

variants.title: Archival reports flood the database
variants.context: The finance team runs heavy monthly reports during business hours and kills checkout latency.
variants.constraint: Read-heavy analytics can accept some lag.
variants.question: Which path is best?
variants.expectedPattern: Use a dedicated replica for reporting queries.

variants.title: Replica lag during major updates
variants.context: The posts table sees a new burst of writes while many users read the same feed.
variants.constraint: A replica is behind the primary and serves stale data.
variants.question: How do you minimize user confusion?
variants.expectedPattern: Route the author’s reads to the primary and keep replicas for heavier read users.
wrongChoices: Add more caches without fixing write path

variants.title: Scaling is good but a single SQL node remains hot
variants.context: You expanded the app layer to three servers, but the database still sees every query.
variants.constraint: Read traffic is the major load, and write traffic is moderate.
variants.question: Which design gives the biggest improvement without a full rewrite?
variants.expectedPattern: Read replicas focused on read traffic with writes remaining on the primary.

variants.title: Celebrity post spike
variants.context: A viral post is read 150,000 times in two minutes, but the database is still serving the same row over and over.
variants.constraint: The content is identical across reads and does not change often.
variants.question: What is your primary optimization?
variants.expectedPattern: Use a cache-aside layer with a TTL and invalidation on update.
wrongChoices: Move all reads to the primary

variants.title: Checkout page hot object
variants.context: A single product is hit by 80% of traffic during a flash sale.
variants.constraint: The page content rarely changes and is highly repetitive.
variants.question: Where should the repeated reads be served from?
variants.expectedPattern: A cache in front of the product read path.

variants.title: Profile storm
variants.context: A popular profile hits the same data repeatedly during a launch campaign.
variants.constraint: Reads dominate; writes are minimal.
variants.question: What pattern offsets the repeated database work?
variants.expectedPattern: Cache profile data and invalidate when updates are made.
wrongChoices: Add a reader-only database without caching
Move profile state into local memory

variants.title: Inventory freshness
variants.context: Inventory values change every few minutes and are read constantly across the app.
variants.constraint: The system can tolerate a small delay but not stale inventory for long.
variants.question: What is the best tradeoff?
variants.expectedPattern: Use a short TTL with invalidation on stock updates.

variants.title: Cache stampede
variants.context: A hot object expires and 8,000 requests miss at once.
variants.constraint: The DB sees a synchronized cold miss from many clients.
variants.question: What prevents the stampede?
variants.expectedPattern: Single-flight refresh or lock around the first miss.

variants.title: Regional traffic burst
variants.context: A local event sends heavy reads to a regional page from one city.
variants.constraint: Most requests hit the same few objects and the origin is far away.
variants.question: Where should the data live for fastest response?
variants.expectedPattern: A regional cache close to users and a shorter TTL on the hot object.

variants.title: Leaderboard freshness
variants.context: A leaderboard updates every 20 seconds but is read continuously.
variants.constraint: A few seconds of staleness is acceptable.
variants.question: What is the right cache policy?
variants.expectedPattern: Short TTL with periodic refresh and invalidation on score changes.

variants.title: Hot user object
variants.context: One user profile object is fetched millions of times per hour, yet the underlying record changes occasionally.
variants.constraint: The data is user-specific and easy to invalidate.
variants.question: How do you keep reads cheap without stale sessions?
variants.expectedPattern: Cache the user metadata with a short expiry and invalidate on update/logout.
wrongChoices: Store it in a single process memory

variants.title: Flash-sale pricing page
variants.context: The same pricing page is hit by thousands of users when a price update happens.
variants.constraint: The pricing data updates infrequently but is read frequently.
variants.question: What is the best design decision?
variants.expectedPattern: Cache product display data and invalidate on pricing updates.

variants.title: Sparse but repeated reads
variants.context: A document or special report is rare but requested heavily for a few minutes.
variants.constraint: A cold object causes a big latency spike and repeated DB hits.
variants.question: How should the system handle the first miss?
variants.expectedPattern: Populate the cache once and serve the rest from memory.
wrongChoices: Use CDN only for dynamic content

variants.title: Global users, single origin
variants.context: Users in Tokyo and New York hit the same app and static assets travel from one origin region.
variants.constraint: Large assets cross an ocean each time and latency climbs.
variants.question: What pattern reduces the latency?
variants.expectedPattern: Serve static assets and media from a CDN close to users.

variants.title: Images consume most of the time
variants.context: Images and scripts dominate page load time for an international audience.
variants.constraint: The page is dynamic but the heavy assets are static.
variants.question: What should be optimized first?
variants.expectedPattern: Deliver static media from edge caches, not the origin.
wrongChoices: Keep all assets on the origin

variants.title: Recent deploy does not appear instantly
variants.context: Users still fetch old static files even after a JS asset is updated.
variants.constraint: Old CDN copies are still cached.
variants.question: What prevents stale assets on deploy?
variants.expectedPattern: Version the asset URL with a hash so the cache sees a new file and fetches it fresh.

variants.title: Game patch day
variants.context: A new game patch is downloaded worldwide and the origin becomes a bottleneck.
variants.constraint: Large artifacts are static and global, but the origin is one region.
variants.question: What is the correct delivery model?
variants.expectedPattern: Use CDN edge distribution for the patch files.
wrongChoices: Route every user to the origin

variants.title: Slow page due to cross-continental static assets
variants.context: A marketing page contains heavy images and CSS served from a single region.
variants.constraint: The dynamic application is fine, but asset delivery is slow.
variants.question: What should be moved closer to users?
variants.expectedPattern: Static media and JS/CSS into edge cache locations.
wrongChoices: Route every request to the same app

variants.title: Origin not handling burst load
variants.context: A product launch causes huge bursts of static asset requests and the origin service is saturated.
variants.constraint: Static content is failing under popular demand.
variants.question: What absorbs the pressure?
variants.expectedPattern: A CDN edge layer that caches and serves static content near the user.

variants.title: Users in Africa wait 500ms for images
variants.context: The app is in Europe and all images are served from a single origin region.
variants.constraint: The bottleneck is physical distance, not compute.
variants.question: How do you reduce the latency?
variants.expectedPattern: Use edge caches in multiple regions and serve local copies of static assets.

variants.title: Slow JS bundle in each market
variants.context: The application sends the same large JS bundle to all users across several regions.
variants.constraint: Each region fetches the same static resource from a distant origin.
variants.question: What is the right optimization?
variants.expectedPattern: Serve the bundle from a nearby CDN edge.
wrongChoices: Move the bundle into the database

variants.title: Back-to-back deployments leave stale edge copies
variants.context: A front-end app is updated every day, but some users receive old CSS files from the edge.
variants.constraint: The CDN keeps caches until they expire.
variants.question: What pattern avoids stale content confusion?
variants.expectedPattern: Versioned asset names with a content hash.

variants.title: Heavy media library
variants.context: A learning platform serves thousands of video thumbnails globally and the origin is overloaded.
variants.constraint: The heavy files are static and heavily reused.
variants.question: What system design fits best?
variants.expectedPattern: Edge caching for thumbnails and media with cache invalidation on content updates.
wrongChoices: Direct data access from the primary DB

variants.title: Payment API delays checkout
variants.context: The checkout endpoint calls a payment provider synchronously and waits on every call.
variants.constraint: The dependency is slow and thread-blocking.
variants.question: What makes request latency recover?
variants.expectedPattern: Enqueue the payment work and return quickly to the user.
wrongChoices: Move the API code into the browser

variants.title: Email sends hang the request path
variants.context: Emails are sent during signup and each request waits for SMTP completion.
variants.constraint: External email sending is slow and often unreliable.
variants.question: What should happen after the user account is created?
variants.expectedPattern: Persist a work item and process it asynchronously.

variants.title: Thumbnails generate too slowly
variants.context: Users upload photos and the app renders thumbnails inline in the request path.
variants.constraint: Thumbnail generation is slow and deferrable.
variants.question: What is the correct design?
variants.expectedPattern: Store the upload, enqueue the thumbnail job, and respond immediately.
wrongChoices: Render thumbnails in the request thread
Cache the upload in the browser
Queue thumbnails without storing the original

variants.title: Pay later crash
variants.context: A worker crashes after charging a card but before acknowledging the message.
variants.constraint: The queue may redeliver the same job.
variants.question: How do you avoid charging twice?
variants.expectedPattern: Use idempotency keys and a safe deduplication strategy.
wrongChoices: Let the request handle the charge

variants.title: Flash sale on the checkout system
variants.context: Payment, email, and order processing happen inside the request while the sale peaks.
variants.constraint: Downstream dependencies are slow and the pool is exhausting threads.
variants.question: What is the right architectural move?
variants.expectedPattern: Queue the expensive downstream tasks and make the request path short.

variants.title: Background workers back up
variants.context: The queue is growing and workers are falling behind under a sudden spike.
variants.constraint: Work is queueing faster than it can be processed.
variants.question: What should be added to prevent collapse?
variants.expectedPattern: Backpressure, retry policies, worker parallelism, and workload prioritization.

variants.title: Complex order processing
variants.context: After a user places an order, the platform calculates taxes, emits notifications, and updates a ledger.
variants.constraint: These steps do not need to complete before the user receives confirmation.
variants.question: How should the order flow be modeled?
variants.expectedPattern: Acknowledge the order quickly, then process the downstream work asynchronously.
wrongChoices: All work on the web request

variants.title: Queue message duplication
variants.context: A message is processed twice because a worker crashes before acknowledging it.
variants.constraint: At-least-once delivery is expected.
variants.question: What safety property must the job handler provide?
variants.expectedPattern: Idempotent processing so duplicate messages do not cause duplicate side effects.

variants.title: User places order but waits too long
variants.context: The order request waits for analytics, tax calculation, and three downstream APIs before returning a response.
variants.constraint: Only the order status is needed immediately.
variants.question: How do you improve user experience without losing correctness?
variants.expectedPattern: Queue non-critical follow-up work and acknowledge the order quickly.
wrongChoices: Wait for all APIs in the request

variants.title: Crashes during message processing
variants.context: A worker starts processing a message, fails mid-way, and the queue redelivers it.
variants.constraint: The side effect is not safe to repeat unless designed carefully.
variants.question: What must you design for?
variants.expectedPattern: Idempotent handlers, retry limits, and observational state.

variants.title: One tenant dominates a shard
variants.context: A single tenant creates 70% of all writes, but the data is stored in one shard.
variants.constraint: The hottest user still produces a hotspot.
variants.question: What is the correct fix?
variants.expectedPattern: Repartition by tenant or key so the hotspot is spread across several shards.

variants.title: Hot key in a hash range
variants.context: One user or key is accessed far more than others, causing one shard to saturate.
variants.constraint: The shard assignment is not balanced enough.
variants.question: What pattern addresses the bottleneck?
variants.expectedPattern: A better sharding strategy or key distribution that avoids hotspots.

variants.title: Large user table under heavy writes
variants.context: An application table keeps growing and a single database shard eventually shows 95% CPU.
variants.constraint: The data is still concentrated in one partition.
variants.question: How do you reduce the hotspot?
variants.expectedPattern: Shard the table based on a stable key or tenant distribution.
wrongChoices: Keep a single DB and increase memory
Route all traffic to a queue

variants.title: Cross-shard fan-out gets expensive
variants.context: The app starts sharding by user but some requests need data from many shards at once.
variants.constraint: A common query now touches multiple partitions.
variants.question: What is the tradeoff?
variants.expectedPattern: Revisit the access pattern and keep hot data local to avoid heavy cross-shard queries.

variants.title: New tenant creates skew after launch
variants.context: A new customer becomes very active overnight and one shard absorbs most traffic.
variants.constraint: Static shard layout is not resilient to skew.
variants.question: What should happen?
variants.expectedPattern: Rebalance or re-shard before the hotspot becomes permanent.
wrongChoices: Add a cache as the only defense

variants.title: Orders table struggles under broad writes
variants.context: Millions of orders are stored in one table and write traffic is spread more evenly than expected, yet one shard is still overloaded.
variants.constraint: The partitioning key is poorly chosen.
variants.question: What design mistake caused it?
variants.expectedPattern: The key choice creates uneven distribution and a hotspot despite multiple shards.

variants.title: Heavy read and write imbalance
variants.context: One shard gets all the writes and the others sit mostly idle.
variants.constraint: The app is horizontally scaled but the data model is still skewed.
variants.question: What does the system need to do?
variants.expectedPattern: Improve partitioning strategy so the read and write workload is spread more evenly.

variants.title: Queueing data on same shard
variants.context: Every new order is placed on the same partition because the sharding key is not random enough.
variants.constraint: Data is not evenly distributed across consumers.
variants.question: What should be changed?
variants.expectedPattern: Choose a better sharding key or a consistent hashing strategy that spreads the load.
wrongChoices: Move the queue before the database

variants.title: Shard growth after customer expansion
variants.context: One business customer expands quickly and all of its data starts landing in the same shard.
variants.constraint: A large tenant becomes the data hotspot.
variants.question: How do you keep the system healthy?
variants.expectedPattern: Split that tenant’s data across multiple shards or use a more granular key distribution.
wrongChoices: Keep all of one tenant in a single partition

variants.title: Geo-based partition seems simple but fails
variants.context: Data is partitioned by region, but one region’s traffic is far higher than the others.
variants.constraint: The partition map is static and some regions are much hotter than the rest.
variants.question: What is the design flaw?
variants.expectedPattern: Hot regions still need a balance strategy; geography alone does not prevent skew.
wrongChoices: Hot regions should never be used

variants.title: User updates profile and refreshes immediately
variants.context: The primary database accepts a profile update, but a read goes to a replica that is still stale.
variants.constraint: Replication is asynchronous and users expect freshness.
variants.question: What keeps the experience correct?
variants.expectedPattern: Read-your-own-writes logic for that user or a short freshness window on their reads.
wrongChoices: Block all reads until replication catches up

variants.title: Follower lags behind leader
variants.context: A replica is behind and serves the old version of a post while the author refreshed the page.
variants.constraint: The rest of the system accepts eventual consistency.
variants.question: Which read behavior is appropriate?
variants.expectedPattern: Read the author’s writes from the primary or a fresh path.
wrongChoices: Force all reads to wait on the leader

variants.title: Regional failover creates stale data
variants.context: A user in a secondary region reads a profile while failover is happening and sees old data.
variants.constraint: Some replicas are behind during failover.
variants.question: What is the right system behavior?
variants.expectedPattern: Use lag-aware routing and a freshness policy for critical reads.
wrongChoices: Always read from the zone with the most replicas

variants.title: Order status appears stale after update
variants.context: The user updates order status, then reads the order immediately and sees an older state.
variants.constraint: The system is eventually consistent but needs better user experience.
variants.question: What is the correct tradeoff?
variants.expectedPattern: Provide fresh reads for the same user session or user-specific workflow.
wrongChoices: Explain the lag to the user
Make all users wait for strong consistency

variants.title: User sees stale post after comment
variants.context: A user submits a comment and sees a stale thread because the read route goes to a non-authoritative replica.
variants.constraint: The app is optimized for availability and throughputs.
variants.question: How do you preserve trust?
variants.expectedPattern: Sessions or user identity should use a fresh read path for recent writes.
wrongChoices: Move all writes to the edge

variants.title: Global reads feel inconsistent
variants.context: Users in different regions do not see the same state at the same timestamp.
variants.constraint: The system is distributed and sync is not instant.
variants.question: What is the core principle?
variants.expectedPattern: Eventual consistency is acceptable if the system makes freshness guarantees explicit for the active user and critical flows.
wrongChoices: All reads must be fully global strong consistency
All data must be in one region

variants.title: User deletion reads stale content
variants.context: A user deletes a post and immediately reloads a page that still shows it on a follower.
variants.constraint: Deletion and visibility updates are asynchronous.
variants.question: How do you avoid the bug?
variants.expectedPattern: Use a freshness-aware read path and metadata-based invalidation for the actor’s own actions.
wrongChoices: Keep deletes in a queue only
Wait for global sync before deletion is visible

variants.title: Cached profile update appears one minute later
variants.context: Users update profile preferences and still see the old page for a minute because the cache is serving an older value.
variants.constraint: The cache is valid but the user wants immediate freshness.
variants.question: What is the right compromise?
variants.expectedPattern: Invalidate or refresh the cache for that user immediately and keep a bounded TTL for others.
wrongChoices: Do nothing and tell users to refresh

variants.title: Social feed shows outdated items
variants.context: An item is posted and appears on the feed of the posting user only after a delay.
variants.constraint: The system balances availability and replica lag.
variants.question: How do you handle the user expectation?
variants.expectedPattern: Ensure the writer sees the post immediately from a fresh source while followers accept eventual consistency.
wrongChoices: Update all replicas before the feed is visible
Block writes until all region replicas sync
Ignore the lag as acceptable for all users

variants.title: Web app modifies account settings in one region
variants.context: The user edits a setting, then reads the account page from another region and sees a stale value.
variants.constraint: Regional consistency is eventually convergent but not instant.
variants.question: What is the honest design answer?
variants.expectedPattern: Use a bounded freshness policy for the active user and explain that global equality is not guaranteed instantly.
wrongChoices: Do nothing and accept stale reads
Lock the platform on every write
